title: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'
description: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA a
body: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA and navigating the next chapter of my career with a focus on prestige and financial success. But soon after relocating from Kentucky to California in October 2021, I burned out. I had transitioned into a remote healthcare marketing role, living on the West Coast but still working East Coast hours and completing my second year of business school from afar. While everyone around me seemed to be heading to the beach and enjoying the sunshine, I spent my days inside, glued to a computer screen.The dog walker I followed online seemed to have everything I was craving: fresh air, movement, flexibility and a job that didn't revolve around emails and Zoom meetings.During a long drive, I joked with my husband, "I think I'm going to quit my job and walk dogs." The joke quickly became a plan.My season as a professional dog walkerWithin the span of just a few weeks in the spring of 2022, I quit my job, graduated from business school, traveled to Europe for an old roommate's wedding and then flew to Texas to speak at the Latino Franchise Symposium. While I was there, I created my Rover profile. I highlighted my experience volunteering at animal shelters in college, pet sitting for friends and caring for animals throughout my life.Before I even made it back home to California, I had my first meet-and-greet scheduled with a potential client. Shortly after, I landed my first booking. I was thrilled.At first, I intentionally priced my services below what seemed typical in my area to build reviews, charging about $15 for a drop-in visit and about $17 for a 30-minute walk. Some days I had just one client. I was able to start small because I had savings to tide me over, along with a partner whose job provided steady income and benefits.My goal was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.Courtesy of Sally SimmonsStill, I treated it like a real business from day one. I accepted nearly every opportunity that came my way, taking dogs on midday walks, housesitting on weekends and boarding dogs in my apartment.I sent thoughtful updates to the dog owners filled with photos, detailed notes and plenty of emojis. I shared bathroom break tallies, funny moments and anything unusual they should know. If I stayed overnight, I brought in packages, cleaned up after myself and made sure their home looked exactly as they had left it.My goal wasn't simply to complete the booking. It was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.The reviews started rolling in. As my profile gained traction, I gradually increased my rates, eventually charging $23 for a drop-in visit and $84 for overnight stays. By the time I left the platform four months later, I had earned a five-star rating with 30 reviews, built a roster of recurring clients and filled my calendar.Walking dogs gave me space to think and reflect on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.Christina Locopo | CNBC Make It; Courtesy of Sally SimmonsOne of my favorite memories came when a family asked me to care for their dogs during their wedding weekend. I spent two and a half days at a beautiful resort and dressed the dogs in tiny tuxedos before they walked down the aisle.It reminded me that this work was about helping families enjoy some of the biggest moments of their lives with peace of mind. Years later, we're still friends. They now have a daughter, and my daughter and I recently attended her first birthday party.A new definition of successSome days I walked more than eight miles, logging over 18,000 steps as I explored neighborhoods I otherwise never would have discovered. I spent hours outside instead of sitting behind a desk. Sometimes I listened to podcasts or music. Other times, I simply enjoyed the quiet.Those walks gave me space to think. I reflected on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.Before Rover, success meant getting promotions, landing bigger clients and climbing the corporate ladder. Walking dogs challenged that definition. I realized I didn't want to chase an impressive title as much as I wanted to chase a lifestyle that gave me energy.Ironically, it was during one of those walks that I received the phone call offering me the marketing job I still have today. I paused on the sidewalk, accepted the offer and then finished the walk.I put a photo of me and my husband holding our own pets (left) on my Rover profile. Long after my dog-walking era, I stayed friends with the dogs Tofu and Noodles (right) and their humans.Courtesy of Sally SimmonsReturning to marketing wasn't a difficult decision. By then, I was pregnant with my first daughter and needed the stability, benefits and predictable income that came with a full-time role. When an excited dog chasing a squirrel pulled me to the ground early in my pregnancy, it became clear that my season as a professional dog walker was coming to an end.Still, I think about those four months often. People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had.It reminded me that passion is visible, no matter what kind of work you're doing. It reinforced that the skills that matter most — showing up, listening, caring deeply, building trust and making small, consistent changes — translate to every career.And even though I'm back in marketing, my days look different than they did before my dog-walking era. These days, you'll find me logging off at 5 p.m. to go play outside with my family before dinner, walking near the ocean after a hard week, having kitchen dance parties to shake off the day, taking calls while walking my own dog or squeezing in a lunchtime workout. The fresh air and sense of presence give me the balance I craved when I was glued to screens on a schedule dictated by someone else's time zone.Those four months taught me something my MBA never could: Success isn't just about finding a job that sounds impressive. It's about building a life you genuinely enjoy living, even if it doesn't look like the one you originally imagined.Sally Simmons is a marketing leader and holistic health coach based in California. After years building strategies for global brands, she found unexpected lessons about business, connection and success during a four-month chapter as a professional dog walker. Today, she brings those lessons into her work helping people create healthier, more balanced lives.

schema.headline: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'

title: In pictures: Protests over inequality, rising living costs turn violent across France
description: Protests across France over a worsening cost-of-living crisis and growing inequality descended into violence for a second straight weekend.France's In
body: Protests across France over a worsening cost-of-living crisis and growing inequality descended into violence for a second straight weekend.France's Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests in several major cities, including Paris.After rioters set fire to the historic city hall in Limoges and looters smashed supermarkets and luxury boutiques in Lyon last weekend, French authorities greatly stepped up security ahead of Saturday's protests.In Paris on Saturday, riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, Reuters quoted a security official as saying.In France's second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police. The confrontations continued after sunset, and police said looters raided two jewelry shops, according to a Reuters report.Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Nantes and Nice, according to the agency.However, the violence was still less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in a number of French cities.The demonstrations began last month as a group of high school students in suburban Paris lamented poor school conditions, including teacher shortages and unsatisfactory facilities. The demonstrations have since grown and evolved into nationwide protests.France's economic and political woes have sharply raised the cost of government borrowing. The yield on its 10-year bond rose above 5% for the first time since 2002 this week, settling around 5.03% on Friday.Some investors fear the country's debt problems could spread to the rest of the euro zone.Protesters and police face off during a demonstration against the rising cost of living in Rennes, France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Vernault Quentin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA demonstrator wearing goggles and a keffiyeh over their face as tear gas spreads across the street during a protest over education funding and rising living costs in Paris, France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Clement Souchet/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA group of police officers from a unit of the motorised anti-violence squad (BRAV-M) caught in a cloud of tear gas, Tension and clashes between violent demonstrators and police forces on the Cours de Vincennes towards the end of the march, Act 2 of the protests against the high cost of living, in support of purchasing power, the protection of public services, and fiscal and social justice, in Paris, France on October 24, 2026.  (Photo by Amaury Cornu / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Amaury Cornu | Afp | Getty ImagesPortrait of a father and his young son posing together during a demonstration, the boy holding a handwritten cardboard placard reading LES COLLEGIENS ON EST LA ! (We are here, too, as middle school students!), in Paris, France, on October 24, 2026. Initially driven by high school students demanding better learning conditions, the movement has also brought together younger pupils and their families, highlighting the involvement of different generations in defending education and shaping their future. (Photo by Aruallan / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Aruallan | Afp | Getty ImagesIn the crowd, a protester holds a sign that reads In 2026, democracy has two tools, the baton and Article 49.3, in Nantes, western France, on October 24, 2026. A demonstration known as Act 2, organized by high school students, politicians, labor unions, and the Yellow Vests, in support of the right to protest, against the high cost of living, and for better conditions in education, work, and daily life, under heavy police surveillance. (Photo by Maylis Rolland / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Maylis Rolland | Afp | Getty ImagesAs the procession passes beneath the emergency room of the university hospital, a protester holds up a sign that reads Eat the rich, in Nantes, western France, on October 24, 2026. A demonstration known as Act 2, organized by high school students, politicians, labor unions, and the Yellow Vests, in support of the right to protest, against the high cost of living, and for better conditions in education, work, and daily life, under heavy police surveillance. (Photo by Maylis Rolland / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Maylis Rolland | Afp | Getty ImagesA protester holds a sign that reads, I dream of another world, in Nantes, western France, on October 24, 2026. A demonstration known as Act 2, organized by high school students, politicians, labor unions, and the Yellow Vests, in support of the right to protest, against the high cost of living, and for better conditions in education, work, and daily life, under heavy police surveillance. (Photo by Maylis Rolland / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Maylis Rolland | Afp | Getty ImagesThree demonstrators wearing Spider-Man costumes or masks point at one another as other participants watch and record the scene during a protest for increased education funding and against rising living costs in Paris, France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Clement Souchet/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesDemonstrators carry large hand-painted banners during a march calling for increased funding for schools and universities and measures against rising living costs in Paris, France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Clement Souchet/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesPolice officers carrying batons and shields face demonstrators gathered on a pavement, several with their hands raised, during a protest for increased education funding and against rising living costs in Paris, France, on October 24, 2026. (Photo by Clement Souchet/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAround 800,000 people demonstrated across France, including 250,000 in Paris, according to the CGT. The march in Paris began at 2 pm from the Porte d'Italie and headed for the Porte de Vincennes after the route was changed by the Police Headquarters at the last minute. October 24, 2026. (Photo by Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFrench riot police walk in a street amid clashes with protesters during an authorized demonstration organized by labor unions in Paris as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in France, on Oct. 24, 2026.Dylan Martinez | Reuters

title: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk’s claim that its military violated Starlink terms during drone operations
description: Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat positio
body: Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026.Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA Ukrainian official disputed SpaceX CEO Elon Musk's claim that Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service, prompting the company to restrict Ukraine's access to the high-speed satellite technology.Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote an online post on Sunday contesting Musk's reason for temporarily throttling Ukraine's access to high-speed service from SpaceX's Starlink satellite communication systems. Ukrainian officials previously said the restrictions disrupted the country's military drone services and left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks.Musk on Saturday claimed in a post on X that the "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people."Beskrestnov pushed back on Musk's allegation, arguing that pre-existing restrictions on the systems would have made it "physically impossible" for Ukraine to use Starlink in the types of strikes the SpaceX CEO described."It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine," Beskrestnov wrote in a post on Telegram, noting that Starlink's civilian system in Ukraine "does not function over the territory of Russia" and that Ukrainian drones operating with Starlink have had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h (roughly 43 to 56 miles per hour) for months."Consequently, it is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations," Beskrestnov wrote.Ukraine officials acknowledged on Saturday that high-speed service for SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems had been restored. The country has blamed that restricted service for disrupting its drone air defense capabilities during frequent Russian air attacks.Starshield is SpaceX's military-focused satellite network for government and national security use, built on technology developed for Starlink, the company's broader commercial satellite internet network.Before Musk acknowledged that he had restricted the systems, confusion and speculation abounded over who ordered the high-speed service changes.At one point, Musk wrote in a social media post that the U.S. government was behind the decision, though President Donald Trump claimed he had no knowledge of the decision. Ukrainian officials have also said Starlink or the U.S. had imposed the restrictions without warning, leaving the country blindsided. Musk has not explained the reported lack of notification to Ukraine before his company implemented the restrictions.Musk and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.The restrictions on Starlink and Starshield in war-torn Ukraine have driven Ukraine and its allies to seek or build alternative, "sovereign" satellite communication systems. Poland's Deputy Minister of National Defense, Cezary Tomczyk, discussed his country's plans on a podcast called Influence Zone (Strefa Influenceów) earlier this month. Ukraine also announced partnerships with Norway and Finland's mobile giant Nokia, as well as satellite maker ICEYE, to develop alternatives.Beyond Ukraine, several countries are also exploring sovereign systems. The European Union is building IRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but it doesn't expect its first launches until 2029.SpaceX's Starlink generated $5.25 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue from consumer Starlink subscribers totaled $3.12 billion, while the company generated $2.13 billion from government and enterprise customers during the quarter.A wide array of customers, including non-government entities, the governments of Poland and France, and the Pentagon, have paid SpaceX to provide its Starlink and Starshield hardware and wireless internet services to Ukraine.

schema.headline: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk’s claim that its military violated Starlink terms during drone operations

title: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
description: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, on May 17, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesA drug from Amgen could
body: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, on May 17, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesA drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca, a study found.Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed."I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility." The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years. Using Imdelltra earlier Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone. Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it. Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer. Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches. Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own. She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread. In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since. "I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

schema.headline: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer

title: Brazil's Lula wins historic presidential election; Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
description: SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - OCTOBER 24: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT)
body: SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - OCTOBER 24: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) waves a Brazil flag during a rally ahead of the presidential runoff at Avenida Paulista on October 24, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.  Alexandre Schneider | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president, overturning a first-round deficit to beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff that split the country almost evenly.Lula took 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with nearly all ballots counted on Sunday. The results are also historic, as it's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round. Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, saying he would seek the annulment of the outcome, Reuters reported. He also said a ruling by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting for two hours was "unacceptable," according to the report.  The election process was marred by allegations of voter suppression, with Lula's campaign reporting suspended public transportation in some key areas, prompting the court to extend voting by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign had also requested an extension, citing heavy rains that shut polling stations in the south, a right-wing stronghold.  The victory of the 80-year-old leftist, who had trailed in the first round, blocks a rightward shift in Latin America that U.S. President Donald Trump has backed. Lula is set to govern from 2027 to 2030, facing a Congress where Bolsonaro's Liberal Party holds the largest bench in decades, and with substantial public debt that he must stabilize. watch nowBrazil, under Lula's leadership, has grappled with worsening fiscal health and mounting public debt driven by elevated cost of servicing the debt and rigid mandatory spending. Gross debt reached 82.9% of the country's GDP in August, the highest since March 2021, according to the Central Bank of Brazil. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) plunged nearly 20% in overnight trading following Lula's win, before paring losses, last down 18%.Analysts had expected a rally in Brazilian assets before Sunday's election results, with Bolsonaro holding a narrow lead earlier this month. Chris Turner, Global Head of Markets and Regional Head of Research for UK & CEE at ING, had forecast both the currency and bond markets to rally, citing Bolsonaro's fiscal austerity and deregulation. Lula's victory came the same day as Serbia's long-serving strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat in a parliamentary election to the student-led opposition movement, ending 14 years of leadership.

schema.headline: Brazil's Lula wins historic presidential election; Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede

title: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections
description: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesU.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East
body: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesU.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report, and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu. Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report.The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel. watch now

schema.headline: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections

title: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs
description: The Audi logo can be seen on a car dealership in Manhattan. Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmak
body: The Audi logo can be seen on a car dealership in Manhattan. Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmaker's plans for a new $4 billion plant in Georgia on Sunday, calling it a business decision aimed at growing sales and reducing exposure to U.S. tariffs.The plant, set to be Audi's first in the U.S., was announced Saturday by President Donald Trump during a rally in Georgia, near where the Volkswagen-owned luxury brand plans to build the new SUV-producing facility."We have significantly greater ambitions for Audi in America," Audi CEO Gernot Dollner said during a media roundtable Sunday. "The United States is the second largest premium market in the world, and today we are not fully exploiting this potential. We are changing that."The announcement comes amid an intense restructuring of its VW parent company, including plans to cut 50,000 jobs and close four German plants, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and ​2034.Dollner, who joined Trump at the rally, said the decision for a plant in the U.S. was years in the making, with more than 70 locations evaluated over "many months" and "intense" negotiations with public officials."This is not a decision against Germany. Germany remains the backbone of Audi," Dollner said. "We develop our cars here. Our technologies are created here, and Georgia does not take any task away from us in Germany."watch nowDollner said localized production is the best decision for the brand, which has struggled in sales this decade amid rising operational costs and Trump's tariffs on vehicles from Germany and other countries into the U.S. Current tariffs on vehicles from Germany are 15%, down from 25%.Last year, U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion), as it imports all its vehicles for the U.S. market from Europe or Mexico.Dollner said the Trump administration asked Audi to announce the new plant at the Georgia rally promoting Republicans ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections."It was … a three-year project that, at the end, by coincidence, led to that moment yesterday," he said Sunday. "With respect of the office and country, we joined the invitation."Dollner noted Audi is the last major German luxury brand to establish U.S. production after Mercedes-Benz and BMW.The company said the Georgia plant is expected to begin production of Audi's Q7, Q8 and Q9 in the early 2030s. The plant would have the capacity to produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually, roughly half of which the automaker said will be exported outside the U.S."This is to make Audi obviously a significant player here in the U.S. market," said Audi of America President Vito Paladino during the roundtable. He also said additional details on U.S. investments and production are forthcoming.Audi's U.S. deliveries were roughly flat through the third quarter of this year, following a 16% decline from 2024 to 2025.

schema.headline: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs

title: Should you travel together? Ask these questions before booking: 'It'll save you time, money and disappointment'
description: Blow-up fights at the Colosseum, tears atop Mount Kilimanjaro and clashes over the window seat: Incompatible travel buddies can ruin a vacation. As ex
body: Blow-up fights at the Colosseum, tears atop Mount Kilimanjaro and clashes over the window seat: Incompatible travel buddies can ruin a vacation. As experts in friendship, travel and decision-making, we know that the stresses and complications of travel, not to mention the near-infinite number of decisions you have to make, can put a lot of pressure on a relationship that was perfectly delightful within a 10-mile radius of your homes. There's a reason that people tell you to travel with someone before you marry them! Thirty-five percent of travelers found that they weren't compatible with a travel buddy, according to a Booking.com survey conducted in July of 1,253 U.S. adults who'd gone away overnight within the last 12 months. Twenty-one percent of respondents had even left a trip part-way through because of their travel partner, and a bad vacation made 28% think about ending the relationship or friendship with their ill-suited travel companion.The problem is that we can have different, unsaid expectations of what a getaway might entail: Does one person want every day booked dawn-to-dusk with activities, while the other wants to lounge in the hotel spa until cocktail hour? Does someone want to go all out with seafood towers and Champagne, while the rest of the group prefers to nosh on convenience store hot dogs and guzzle local beer? Not every friend, romantic partner or family member is the right travel partner for you. And it'll save you time, money and disappointment to figure that out before you plan your itinerary. Ask these travel compatibility questions before bookingWe've created a quiz to help you quickly determine compatibility with your prospective travel partner so you can sidestep potential headaches down the line. Here are six of the most important questions:1. What kind of accommodations are you imagining? Are you comfortable sharing?Start with the basics. Some of us can conk out in the middle of the nightclub; others need a white noise machine, blackout curtains and a room to ourselves. The hotels, hostels or apartments you visit on your trip are key to compatibility on the road — it's hard to have a blissful holiday when you're exhausted from someone else's snoring.2. Do you check your luggage?The carry-on vs. checked luggage debate will never die, and this is one difference it's wise to hash out in advance. No one wants to spend days carefully choosing their most stain-resistant T-shirts to tuck into a backpack only to see the other person arrive at the check-in desk with two maxed-out suitcases. This doesn't have to be a holiday dealbreaker, but discuss it so everyone knows what to expect.3. What does your dream vacation look like? Is your dream vacation full of leisurely days, wandering around, popping into shops and cafes that look interesting and taking afternoon naps? Or is your dream vacation full of museums, restaurants, activities and movement?For some people, a "vacation" means downtime, with few planned activities and lots of white space to do whatever feels appealing in the moment. For others, there's no point in leaving home unless you're going to maximize your time, and leaving a destination without visiting every dot on your dense Google Map is a wasted holiday.4. How long does it take you to get ready in the morning?This might seem insignificant, but more than one trip has been strained by a long morning routine. One person is straightening their hair and gluing on eyelashes; the other is wearing the same outfit they had on yesterday and tapping their foot, impatiently waiting to get going. If you're incompatible on this point but still want to travel together, we suggest deciding on a strategy in advance. Maybe it's okay for one person to go out and explore, get coffee or eat the hotel breakfast alone, or the traveler who takes longer to get ready commits to setting an alarm for 45 minutes before their companion.5. How much do you expect to spend?Do you prefer to travel on the cheap? Or do you not get out of bed for fewer than five stars? In the Booking.com survey, 35% of respondents had argued over money with their travel buddy.Budget considerations might be the most important thing to discuss before committing to anything. Ideally, you'd each set a budget for the trip, a number you'd be entirely comfortable spending, and then compare to see how far apart you are. If one person is dreaming of an airport limousine pickup and the other person is planning to squirrel away bread rolls from the hotel breakfast to eat for lunch, you might be better off on different trips.6. Will you be offended if your travel companion listens to music using headphones or opens a book?Ever been stuck in an airplane seat next to someone who just won't shut up? Compatible travel isn't just about similar taste in food and accommodations. You're going to be spending a lot of time with your travel buddy. So before you get on that airport shuttle, have a quick chat: Are we both okay with doing our own thing during the tedious parts of the journey? Or does one of you expect that you'll be "on" 24 hours a day and get their feelings hurt if the other prefers to zone out to a podcast?Compare your answers and make the callOnce each potential traveler has answered the questions, review them together, discuss and make a decision about traveling together — or not.If too many differences come up, shake hands and agree to keep your hangouts local.If you're mostly on the same page, see if you can plan a trip that works for both of you. For example, if your ideal activities or costs don't match up, maybe one day you split up and just meet for dinner, or you set a restaurant budget together in advance rather than figuring it out on the fly and coming home to huge credit card bills.If you're giving the same answer for every question, then you have our congratulations. Go forth and book those tickets!Anna Goldfarb is a friendship expert and author of "Modern Friendship: How to Nurture Our Most Valued Connections," a Next Big Idea Club Must-Read. She writes the Substack Friendship Explained. She's been featured in the New York Times, The Atlantic, The Washington Post, WIRED, Oprah Daily, Goop and more. Follow her on Instagram.   Nell Wulfhart has been helping people make big (and small!) decisions since 2013. Her clients have included politicians, hedge fund managers, Netflix executives, poets, parents, med students and many more. You can listen in on her coaching sessions on her podcast, The Decision Coach. Find her at decisioncoach.com.

schema.headline: Should you travel together? Ask these questions before booking: 'It'll save you time, money and disappointment'

title: What Democrats and Republicans fear most about each other: CNBC survey has the answers
description: watch nowIf Democrats take over Congress, Republican voters are worried they'll move too far to the left and enact socialist policies. If Republicans
body: watch nowIf Democrats take over Congress, Republican voters are worried they'll move too far to the left and enact socialist policies. If Republicans keep control, Democrats fret about President Donald Trump having unchecked power.Those are the findings from a new CNBC poll that shows what each side of the political divide fears about the other as the midterm election looms. Republicans in the survey also say they worry about weakened border security and higher taxes under a Democratic Congress. Democrats say they're concerned about continued Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations and ongoing military efforts in Iran under a Republican one."That totally shows the polarization … and the fear that one side is going to completely undo the agenda of the other," Ron Bonjean, a Republican strategist and co-founder of ROKK Solutions, said of the results. "What Republicans are worried about is that Democrats are going to go back to the way it was during the Biden administration."The results of the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey — conducted between Oct. 14 and 18 and including 1,000 registered voters — could serve as a warning for both parties after the election. Both Democrats and Republicans have struggled with low favorability amid widespread distrust of the government.If Democrats lurch too far to the left and adopt Democratic Socialists of America policies, they could squander the gains some forecasts project they could make in many heavily Republican parts of the country, said Lucas Holtz, a senior political advisor at Third Way, a center-left think tank. "They should not misread their mandate if they hope to retain the inroads that they're making this cycle with Latino voters, with working-class voters, who they have been hemorrhaging cycle after cycle," Holtz said. And Republicans should understand that voters in this moment want to change course, Bonjean said."Voters absolutely want change from the way things are going now, but they also don't want to go back to the way things were when Democrats ran Washington," Bonjean said. "The branding is so bad on the Democratic side, and it's not great on the Republican side."Respondents were able to select up to two of their biggest concerns in the event that Democrats or Republicans control Congress, which don't necessarily indicate their top electoral priorities. The CNBC survey by Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies separately asked people to name the most important issues facing the country. In answering that question, affordability issues ranked highly across the political spectrum, while Democrats and independents also listed government corruption as a top priority, and Republicans listed immigration and border security.Still, the concerns expressed by voters about what the opposing party might do in office reflect the messages in the political advertising that is blanketing much of the country in the final days before the midterm election, according to Alex Jacquez, senior vice president of policy, advocacy, and research at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive think tank. Democrats on the campaign trail have hammered Trump for his alleged corruption and Republicans have attempted to paint Democrats as overly progressive."For Democrats, the main attack ads [targeting them] have ... been about DSA and they've been about the cultural issues that Republicans are trying to hit to tie them to a kind of a far-left or radical movement," Jacquez said. "But the overall vibe of the election is still first and foremost about the economy, people tend to blame the president for prices and Congress for enabling him."If Democrats gain control of Congress, 22% of all voters said they are concerned about them failing to bring down prices, including 31% of Democrats, 22% of independents and 15% of Republicans. In the event the GOP retains the gavels in the House and Senate, 24% of voters said they worry whether prices will come down, including 32% of Republicans, 22% of independents and 17% of Democrats.But those worries trail fears about checking Trump and policies associated with the DSA, a political organization that has notched recent wins in places like New York City, Washington and Denver and advocates progressive social and populist economic policies.Of all voters polled, 44% said they fear Trump would be allowed to operate beyond his constitutional power, including 74% of Democrats and 45% of independents. Twenty-eight percent of respondents said they are concerned with the implementation of DSA policies, including 54% of Republicans and 22% of independents.

schema.headline: What Democrats and Republicans fear most about each other: CNBC survey has the answers

title: Marc Lore’s Wonder bets on Texas, automation and user-built restaurants as it mulls IPO
description: watch nowLess than a decade after its founding, food startup Wonder has seen its footprint and valuation soar. Still, the company has even more ambiti
body: watch nowLess than a decade after its founding, food startup Wonder has seen its footprint and valuation soar. Still, the company has even more ambitious plans ahead, like a subscription program to let diners run their own "restaurants," an aggressive expansion in Texas and a potential initial public offering.Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place." Diners can place takeout or delivery orders from its food hall-style locations on the Wonder-branded app or third-party platforms, including Grubhub, which Wonder now owns. As Lore described it to CNBC, "Wonder is a vertically integrated food technology platform to make great food more accessible."To achieve its goal, Wonder plans to open locations in urban, suburban and rural areas nationwide and aims to keep prices lower than the cost of delivered groceries. Thanks to its ownership of Grubhub, Wonder customers who order through the startup's app don't have to pay delivery fees, and its menu prices aren't inflated to cover the cost of commission fees to the delivery platform. Plus, Wonder is automating some of its kitchen functions, like assembling salads and bowls and soon sauces and beverages. The company aims for food preparation and delivery to be fully autonomous by 2040, Lore said. Now, Wonder has to convince diners its platform built on cost savings and choice makes it worth their while in a competitive industry.Lore's lofty vision for Wonder has helped the company raise $3.3 billion to date, from investors like DoorDash, Alphabet's venture arm and Gwyneth Paltrow. Its Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion — just under sandwich chain Subway's sale price two years ago.Wonder's next pitch to investors could be on an IPO road show, assuming that the window for companies across industries to go public reopens in the coming months."[The mission] is really why I want to go public and raise the capital that it'll take to build that kind of generational business, also to have a public currency to be able to do more M&A," Lore said. "But I can't talk about timing."Lore's track recordMarc Lore speaks onstage during The Playbook with David Meltzer at Fanatics Fest NYC 2026 at Jacob Javits Center in New York, July 18, 2026.Daniel Zuchnik | Getty ImagesLore's expertise lies in e-commerce, not restaurants. He helped found the parent company of Diapers.com and sold it in 2010 to Amazon for $545 million. Just six years later, Walmart paid about $3 billion for his follow-up venture, Jet.com. Lore stayed at the retailer until 2021 to accelerate Walmart's e-commerce growth. Basketball fans might also recognize Lore as an owner of the Minnesota Timberwolves. In 2021, he and baseball legend Alex Rodriguez agreed to buy the team for $1.5 billion, although the deal was not finalized until 2025. Lore recently struck a deal to shrink his investment to a minority stake "to focus on his business," Rodriguez said in a statement in August, referring to Wonder.Lore's latest startup began with the idea of bringing food delivery to consumers' homes through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens. The trucks lasted roughly two years before Wonder phased them out in favor of brick-and-mortar locations, which could serve more food options and lower costs. Lore's successful track record has helped him win over investors for Wonder."I joke around at GV that I do enterprise software investing, AI investing and anything that Marc Lore is running as an active CEO," said Dave Munichiello, managing partner of Alphabet's venture capital arm GV, who has known Lore since his Diapers.com days and invested in Jet.com through GV.Lore himself thinks that his vision is the reason for Wonder's billions of dollars of funding. "Everybody eats," he said. "It's defensible from AI."Wonder has spent more than $1 billion on acquisitions, not including the deals where financial details were not disclosed. Its purchases of Grubhub, delivery and logistics provider Relay, meal-kit provider Blue Apron and buzzy New York restaurant concepts have been expensive. But Lore said he sees a "tremendous total addressable market" for Wonder if it's able to sell high-quality food at accessible prices, particularly in exurban and rural areas with few dining options beyond fast food and gas stations. Wonder gets bigger in TexasSign at the entrance to the Wonder store in Midtown Manhattan. Erik Mcgregor | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesFrom Virginia to Massachusetts, 170 Wonder storefronts have appeared over the last three years. Next year, the company plans to enter Texas for the first time — with a goal of at least 100 locations in the state by the end of 2027. Wonder prepares its food at commissary kitchens, then transports it to each individual location, where employees unseal, cook and finish the menu items. Its storefronts are all electric, without gas or venting, so Wonder can quickly move into a new space and cut down on renovations and red tape. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants," including Dabba Indian Kitchen, Tejas Barbecue and Pop Salad. Celebrity chefs including Bobby Flay, Michael Symon and Marcus Samuelsson receive up-front payments and equity in Wonder to let the company use their names for some of those concepts. More recent additions include acquisitions such as Blue Ribbon Fried Chicken and Salt Hank's, brands with established followings.With its wide variety of options housed under one roof, Wonder has drawn comparisons to ghost kitchens, the once-buzzy startups without dine-in seating that flamed out as food delivery orders fell after the Covid pandemic. Once considered a potential disruptor to the restaurant industry, ghost kitchen companies such as Kitchen United have sought bankruptcy protection and wound down their operations.Lore disagrees with the comparison. "You can see there's a front of house [in the] brick and mortar," he said. "You'll see people at lunchtime, sitting there enjoying lunch, so it's not ghost-y in that way. But I think it's also just in the fact that we're vertically integrated."Wonder has never marketed itself as a ghost kitchen, instead calling itself "a new kind of food hall" or a "modern food court" before landing on a "vertically integrated food technology platform."Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to take the next step with Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own "restaurant" based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders. Artificial intelligence will help them make their brand, including name, logo, pricing and recipes. "It could be a restaurant for you and your friends, or you could be an influencer that has a following," Lore said. He wants Wonder Create to democratize restaurant ownership — minus the capital, overhead costs or oversight of kitchen operations. The platform will eventually be available to the public, with users deciding menu items based on Wonder's pantry.Besides Wonder Create, the company is also using AI for another initiative. MEL, a proprietary AI platform, can use a customer's health information, like data from an Oura ring or Whoop tracker or even blood biomarkers, to prepare breakfast, lunch and dinner for its user.MEL is not currently available to Wonder customers, although Lore uses AI to advise his own meals, like the chicken muffin he ate for breakfast on a Tuesday in October.   The quality questionAssorted foods from Wonder.Courtesy: WonderWhile Wonder has won over venture capitalists, the battle for diners' stomachs and wallets is tougher. Budget-conscious consumers have been dining out less often and becoming pickier when they do so. And while food delivery is still more popular than it was before the pandemic, consumers have pulled back on delivery orders compared with their Covid-era peak. Fees and high menu prices, which offset eateries' commission fees with apps, make delivery even more expensive than dining at a restaurant. Plus, some consumers are skeptical about Wonder more specifically. Posts on social media decry the company's food quality and its funding from venture capital. "It's OK, but it's just average," Amir Ings, a 27-year-old living in Philadelphia, said in a TikTok reviewing an order of three tacos from Wonder in late 2025. "My expectations were already in the gutter — it's not as bad as I thought it was going to be, but it's still not great. And I paid like $16 for this, but it should have been no more than $8."Lore told CNBC that Wonder receives thousands of reviews every day from customers, rating the taste, temperature and portion size of their orders on a scale from 1 to 10. Wonder starts its board meetings by talking about taste scores, Munichiello said."We're maniacally focused on food quality .... We're constantly iterating on the meals that score lower, and see over time, the last 12 months, our taste scores have improved, our Google reviews have improved," Lore said. "I do expect food quality to improve as we scale, which is not always the case."Despite lackluster reviews on social media, Wonder has fans. Based on transaction data from Indagari, Wonder had a higher weighted average retention rate — how likely a diner is to return — and higher lifetime value — how much a customer has spent over time — than Cava and Sweetgreen.Plus, Wonder has succeeded with locations in the most competitive markets for restaurants in the country. "They made this company work well in the hardest place in the country to stand up this model: New York," Munichiello said. "You have so much choice in New York."Ultimately, Wonder wants to win over the rest of the U.S. — and public market investors. In March, the company hired Gabrielle Scheibe Rabinovitch, previously at payment processor Worldpay, as its chief financial officer as it prepares to go public. Lore declined to comment on the timing of a potential IPO to CNBC, although he has previously told Fortune that the company will be "ready and prepared to go public early next year."Since buying Blue Apron and Grubhub, Wonder has been operating at a financial loss, The Information previously reported. It plans to bring down the price of its meals by leaning into automation and drone delivery. In the long term, that plan could cut costs, although laying the groundwork won't be cheap.In recent years, investors have grown less tolerant of startups pursuing growth at all costs, according to Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital. To sway investors, unprofitable companies have to show they are taking steps toward profitability — or that the growth will continue long after the IPO.

title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
description: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's
body: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October."Nearly 70% of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates. "In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout. Major AI companies have been warning about the technology's advancing cybersecurity capabilities since April, when Anthropic announced a limited rollout of its powerful model called Mythos. Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company called Hugging Face. Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote in a post on X on Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better."Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told CNBC on Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline."This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become. "While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams."Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this reportWATCH: Chris Krebs on AI discovering cyber vulnerabilities: It’ll get worse before it gets better

schema.headline: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble

title: ‘Ticking time bomb’: The world's pension funds face an ageing crisis
description: Pension funds’ continued exposure and plans to increase allocations come at a time when parts of the private credit market, particularly software-heav
body: Pension funds’ continued exposure and plans to increase allocations come at a time when parts of the private credit market, particularly software-heavy lending, are facing heightened scrutiny.Christopher Furlong | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe world's pension systems are confronting a demographic crisis as longer lifespans and dwindling birth rates threaten to stretch retirement finances, raising questions about their ability to sustain payouts for future generations.Pension offerings generally fall into two categories: defined-benefit plans, which promise retirees a predetermined income, and defined-contribution plans, where payouts depend on accumulated savings and investment returns. Ageing poses different challenges for the two systems: defined-benefit schemes face mounting liabilities as retirees live longer, while defined-contribution members risk outliving their savings, placing greater pressure on funds' investment performance.The problem is "huge, and it's gotten more pronounced over time,” said Sebastien Betermier, executive director at the International Centre for Pension Management, noting that some pension funds have members who have been retired for nearly half a century, aged aged 107 or 108. "The higher the longevity, the more years the pension funds have to cover, and so that immediately comes in as an additional liability," he said. "Think about the cost that it imposes actually on the next generation … it is a ticking time bomb," Betermier told CNBC.The scale of the challenge is laid bare in the 2026 Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index, or MCGPI, report published Tuesday last week. Of the 55 pension systems covered by the index, 43 have fertility rates below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman, while 23 have rates below 1.5.Meanwhile, life expectancy at age 65 in more developed regions has increased by 50.9% since 1950 to about 20 additional years, meaning retirement benefits must now last considerably longer. The number of potential workers supporting older people is also set to decline sharply.“The funding of future pensions and aged care both become more critical as the ratio of workers to retirees continues to decline,” the MCGPI report stated. “Very few systems, as they currently operate, are secure.”The problem is particularly acute for pay-as-you-go pension systems in which contributions from today's workers largely fund benefits for current retirees, leaving them especially vulnerable to a shrinking workforce.The pressures are already evident in the U.S., where the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which finances retirement and survivor benefits for tens of millions of Americans, is projected to exhaust its reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032, according to its latest trustees' report.Everybody is shifting a little more risk where they can. The costs are going up with this demographic shift.Jean-Pierre Aubry Center for Retirement Research at Boston CollegeFully funded pension schemes, which invest contributions from workers and employers to finance future retirement benefits are not immune either.As their members retire and begin drawing down benefits, some funds could find themselves paying out more than they receive in fresh contributions, forcing them to rethink their investment strategies and liquidity needs, MCGPI cautioned.“Future benefit outflows will exceed the level of contributions or premiums ... this financial strain will inevitably grow in the future,” the report highlighted.Rethinking riskThe demographic crunch is reshaping how pension funds invest, with some taking on greater risks to generate the returns needed to meet growing retirement obligations.Many mature funds are already paying out more in benefits than they receive in contributions, forcing them to rely increasingly on investment returns and accumulated assets. In Australia, about a third of superannuation funds recorded negative natural cash flows from assets over a three-year period, meaning benefit payments exceeded contributions, according to a 2025 report by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.Industry watchers say the pressure to generate higher returns has pushed some funds toward riskier and more complex investments, including private equity, infrastructure and private credit."You can try to earn higher returns on your investments, but that's going to require taking on greater levels of risk," said Betermier.Jean-Pierre Aubry, associate director of state and local research at the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, said pension funds were increasingly shifting toward riskier investments, although the extent varied considerably across markets.watch now"I think everybody is shifting a little more risk where they can. The costs are going up with this demographic shift," Aubry said.He pointed to U.S. state and local government pension funds, which hold only about 20% of their assets in bonds, with much of the remainder invested in equities and private assets.Such allocations make U.S. public pension funds considerably more exposed to investment risk than their counterparts in Europe and Canada, he said.Not every pension manager sees ageing as a reason to take bigger bets.David Elias, CEO of Australian pension fund Hostplus said demographic changes were only one of many factors shaping investment decisions.He stressed the importance of maintaining a diversified portfolio across asset classes, geographies and industries, while ensuring that potential returns adequately compensate for the risks involved.Elias also said that governments could find ways to mitigate the pressures of ageing populations, including through immigration policies and technological advances, while demographic shifts themselves could create new investment opportunities."I don't underestimate governments being incredibly creative in terms of dealing with these types of issues," he said. "You know, but they're going to have to address it, no doubt about that."

schema.headline: ‘Ticking time bomb’: The world's pension funds face an ageing crisis

title: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
description: President Donald Trump shows the crowd an executive order he just signed during a campaign rally at Pinnacle Bank Expo Center in Grand Island, Nebrask
body: President Donald Trump shows the crowd an executive order he just signed during a campaign rally at Pinnacle Bank Expo Center in Grand Island, Nebraska, Oct. 5, 2026.Kent Nishimura | Afp | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump has signed an executive order that aims to reduce mortgage costs as rising interest rates and inflation make homeownership less affordable.The order, titled "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People," directs federal agencies to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on eligible future loans and expand a program to make refinancing cheaper, among other actions.In an X post on Thursday, Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte said "millions of Americans will save thousands and thousands of dollars." But it's difficult to know the future consumer impact without more details, according to Keith Gumbinger, vice president of mortgage website HSH.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageCNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approachTrump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donationsThousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher paymentsSocial Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Trump's executive order comes less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with rising costs and housing affordability a major concern among voters. It builds on previous orders to restrict Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes, among other actions.  Homeownership has become less affordable in recent years. In 2025, the monthly payment for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage on a median-priced home was roughly 33% of the median family's income, up from 26% in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's latest Survey of Consumer Finances published in early October.Whether you're a current homeowner or future buyer, here are some of the key things to know about the new executive order.Mortgage insurance changes Conventional loans — mortgages not insured or backed by U.S. government programs — typically require private mortgage insurance, or PMI, when a down payment is less than 20% of the home's purchase price. By contrast, Federal Housing Administration mortgages require mortgage insurance on all loans. Trump's executive order directs the FHFA to create a pilot program that cancels eligible borrowers' mortgage insurance "proactively" once their home equity reaches a certain threshold, according to the White House. This would apply to mortgages originated after the pilot program launches. Currently, conventional loan borrowers can generally remove PMI once their loan balance is below 80% of the purchase price or once they have reached 20% equity, according to Fannie Mae. Once your balance reaches 80% of the original value, you can ask your loan servicer if you're eligible to remove PMI, or they may remove it automatically when your balance reaches 78% of the original value.In a statement Thursday, Seth Appleton, president of U.S. mortgage insurers, an industry trade organization, said: "We commend the President's focus on lowering costs for future homeowners, and the private mortgage insurance industry is proud to already be delivering on that goal."Typically, the cost of PMI can be 0.2% to 2% of the loan annually, but varies based on your down payment size, credit score, amount borrowed and other factors, according to Fannie Mae. For example, if you purchased a $600,000 home with a 10% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.3%, your monthly mortgage insurance could be $351, according to a private mortgage calculator from Freddie Mac. "Most mortgages ... are carrying PMI at this point in time, especially with the way home prices have been and down payments being as small as they've been in recent years," Gumbinger said. During the second quarter of 2026, the median home down payment was 13.7% of the home's purchase price, or $27,100, according to a September report from Realtor.com.Mortgage refinancing costs Trump's executive order also aims to reduce mortgage refinancing costs by making permanent the FHFA's pilot program that waives the lender's title insurance policy and allows "cost-friendly alternatives," according to the White House."I don't know that it's necessarily a game-changer in terms of the cost of housing, which is dictated by home price and mortgage rates at the moment," Gumbinger said. "But you know, every little bit certainly helps."As of Oct. 23, mortgage interest rates for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages were 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac, and refinance demand was down 59% in mid-October, compared with the same week the previous year. watch nowOriginally planned through November 2027, the FHFA pilot was "limited in scope," for refinances with a loan-to-value ratio below 80%, in a handful of states, former FHFA director Sandra Thompson said during a congressional hearing in April 2024. Thompson estimated that consumers could save $500 to $1,500 in closing costs for loans sold under the pilot program.Making the program permanent could save borrowers because the lender's title insurance policy, which is usually required for new loans and refinances, "has always been fairly pricey," Gumbinger said.The lender's fees related to title and title insurance generally make up the largest share of mortgage closing costs, according to a 2025 Urban Institute report.

schema.headline: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers

title: I paid off $11,000 of credit card debt in 18 months while still traveling, shopping and living my life
